Amos 1.summary: Amos begins by identifying himself as a herdsman from Tekoa whose words concern Israel during the reigns of Uzziah and Jeroboam II, two years before an earthquake (Amos 1:1). The LORD's voice is pictured roaring from Zion, making even fruitful landscapes wither (Amos 1:2). A sequence of oracles then names crimes by neighboring nations. Damascus is condemned for brutal treatment of Gilead, including the image of iron threshing instruments (Amos 1:3–5). Gaza and other Philistine centers are condemned for transporting whole communities into captivity and handing them to Edom (Amos 1:6–8). Tyre is charged with betraying a covenant while delivering captives to Edom (Amos 1:9–10). Edom is accused of relentless violence against a brother people (Amos 1:11–12), and Ammon of atrocities against pregnant women in Gilead committed to enlarge its borders (Amos 1:13–15). Each oracle repeats a numeric pattern, "For three transgressions...and for four," a wisdom-saying idiom meaning sin piled upon sin rather than a literal count of exactly four crimes. The central message is that violence, human trafficking, and violated obligations come under God's judgment, including beyond Israel's boundaries.
Amos 1.whereWeAre: Joel ended with a promise that the LORD would dwell in Zion forever, after judging the nations that had wronged his people (Joel 3:18–21). Amos opens the next book by turning that same judgment outward first: a shepherd from Judah announces one oracle after another against Israel's neighbors, Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon, for their cruelty in war. Each oracle names a specific nation, building toward chapter 2, where the same formula turns inward and lands on Judah, then finally on Israel itself.

keyFigures.name: Amos
keyFigures.role: Prophetic speaker from Tekoa. Introduces oracles concerning Israel and its neighbors (Amos 1:1-2)

keyFigures.name: Uzziah and Jeroboam son of Joash
keyFigures.role: Kings used in the opening date. Locate Amos in the period of Judah and Israel's divided monarchies (Amos 1:1)

keyFigures.name: Damascus (Aram), Philistine cities, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon
keyFigures.role: Nations or cities addressed. Accused of specific acts of cruelty, enslavement, and covenant betrayal (Amos 1:3-15)

keyFigures.name: Hazael and Ben-hadad
keyFigures.role: Named Aramean royal house. Named in the judgment oracle against Damascus (Amos 1:4)

keyThemes.explanation: Even nations with no covenant relationship to the LORD are held responsible for how they treat others in war, starting with Damascus's brutal treatment of Gilead (1:3-5).
Gaza and Tyre are condemned specifically for handing entire captured populations over to slavery, treating conquered people as goods to trade rather than as human beings (1:6-10).

Edom's relentless hostility toward a brother people and Ammon's atrocities against pregnant women in Gilead show violence pursued for its own sake or for territorial gain, not merely as a byproduct of war (1:11-15).
Amos introduces his message as the LORD's own roaring voice from Zion, grounding a herdsman's words in divine authority rather than his own standing (1:1-2).

Amos 2.summary: The sequence of judgments continues with Moab, condemned for burning the bones of Edom's king into lime (Amos 2:1–3). Judah is then accused of rejecting the LORD's law and following deceptive falsehoods (Amos 2:4–5). The longest oracle focuses on Israel: people sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, trample the poor, abuse sexual relationships, and misuse pledged garments and wine associated with fines in religious settings (Amos 2:6–8). God recalls bringing Israel from Egypt, destroying the Amorite before them, and raising up prophets and Nazirites (Amos 2:9–11). Yet Israel has pressured Nazirites to drink wine and commanded prophets not to speak (Amos 2:12). A series of images of failed escape and collapsed military strength announces judgment (Amos 2:13–16). The point is that Israel's privileged history increases rather than removes its responsibility for justice and faithful worship.
Amos 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 worked through oracles against five surrounding nations for their cruelty in war (Amos 1:3–15). Chapter 2 completes the sequence with Moab and Judah before landing its longest oracle on Israel itself, a nation that received God's own deliverance from Egypt but now sells the poor for silver and silences the prophets he raised up among them. That indictment carries straight into chapter 3, where Amos explains why Israel's special relationship with God brings stricter accountability rather than protection.

keyFigures.name: Moabites
keyFigures.role: Neighboring people under indictment. Condemned over desecration of a defeated king’s remains (Amos 2:1-3)

keyFigures.name: Judah
keyFigures.role: Southern kingdom. Accused of rejecting the LORD’s instruction (Amos 2:4-5)

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Northern kingdom and main addressee. Accused of economic oppression, religious misconduct, and resistance to prophets (Amos 2:6-16)

keyFigures.name: Amorites
keyFigures.role: People recalled in Israel’s history. Their defeat is presented as part of Israel’s remembered deliverance (Amos 2:9-10)

keyFigures.name: Prophets and Nazirites
keyFigures.role: Groups raised up among Israel. Their treatment illustrates rejection of spiritual accountability (Amos 2:11-12)

keyThemes.explanation: Selling the poor for the price of a pair of sandals and trampling the needy into the dust shows Israel's economic life built on treating vulnerable people as disposable (2:6-7).
Misusing pledged garments and fine money taken as pledges, even beside altars, shows religious settings being used to cover rather than correct injustice (2:7-8).

God recalls destroying the Amorites, bringing Israel from Egypt, and raising up prophets and Nazirites as evidence that Israel's current conduct is a betrayal of grace already given, not simple ignorance (2:9-11).
Pressuring Nazirites to break their vows and ordering prophets not to speak shows Israel actively working to remove the very voices meant to call it back to God (2:11-12).

Amos 3.summary: Amos addresses the whole family brought up from Egypt, declaring that being specially known by God carries a distinctive accountability (Amos 3:1–2). A chain of everyday comparisons asks whether events occur without causes, from two walking together to a lion roaring and a trumpet sounding (Amos 3:3–6). The prophet says that the LORD reveals his purpose to his servants the prophets; when the LORD speaks, Amos must prophesy (Amos 3:7–8). Observers are summoned from Ashdod and Egypt to see oppression and disorder in Samaria (Amos 3:9–10). An adversary will surround the land, stripping strongholds, and only a remnant will be rescued, compared to the remains of an animal torn by a lion (Amos 3:11–12). The condemnation extends to Bethel's altars and the luxurious winter and summer houses adorned with ivory (Amos 3:13–15). The chapter links covenant election, oppression, prophetic warning, and the instability of wealth built on injustice.
Amos 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with Israel's history of deliverance turned into an indictment, since the very people God rescued from Egypt now reject his prophets and oppress the poor (Amos 2:9–12). Chapter 3 explains why that history raises the stakes: being specially known by God brings greater accountability, not immunity, and the LORD must speak through Amos the way thunder follows a lion's roar. The chapter's closing image of Samaria's ivory houses facing ruin carries into chapter 4, where Amos names exactly who lives in those houses and why they will be the first to fall.

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaker of the covenant accusation. Declares judgment and explains the prophet’s compulsion (Amos 3:1-8)

keyFigures.name: Israel (children of Israel)
keyFigures.role: Collective addressees. Their special relationship is presented as increasing accountability (Amos 3:1-2)

keyFigures.name: Amos
keyFigures.role: Prophetic messenger in this oracle. Insists that the LORD reveals his plans to his servants the prophets before compelling Amos himself to speak (Amos 3:7-8)

keyFigures.name: People in Samaria
keyFigures.role: Inhabitants associated with stored violence. Their strongholds and homes are targeted in the oracle (Amos 3:9-15)

keyFigures.name: Observers from Ashdod and Egypt
keyFigures.role: Summoned witnesses. Asked to observe Samaria’s oppression (Amos 3:9)

keyThemes.explanation: Being the one family specially known by God does not exempt Israel from judgment; it is the reason God holds Israel to a stricter account than other nations (3:1-2).
Amos compares his compulsion to prophesy to the involuntary fear caused by a lion's roar, insisting that once God has spoken, silence is not an option for those he sends (3:7-8).
Calling witnesses from Ashdod and Egypt, foreign and often hostile nations, to see Samaria's internal disorder shows oppression so severe that even outsiders would recognize it as wrong (3:9-11).

The image of a shepherd recovering only scraps of a sheep killed by a lion previews how little will remain of Samaria's winter houses, summer houses, and ivory decorations once judgment arrives (3:12-15).

Amos 4.summary: The chapter opens with a sharp denunciation of the prosperous women of Samaria, whom Amos calls "kine of Bashan," who oppress the poor and demand drink (Amos 4:1–3). Judgment is pictured vividly as being dragged away with hooks and fishhooks, like cattle led by force. Amos then delivers an ironic invitation to continue worshiping at Bethel and Gilgal while multiplying transgression (Amos 4:4–5). A repeated refrain follows: shortages of bread, irregular rain, crop diseases and locusts, disease and war, and catastrophic destruction have failed to bring the people back to God (Amos 4:6–11). The warning culminates in the command to prepare to meet God (Amos 4:12), followed by a hymn praising the One who forms mountains, creates wind, and rules day and night (Amos 4:13). The central message is that ritual confidence without justice and a refusal to heed repeated warnings lead toward a decisive confrontation.
Amos 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 closed by condemning the luxury of Samaria's winter and summer houses as evidence of coming judgment (Amos 3:13–15). Chapter 4 names exactly who enjoys that luxury, the wealthy women of Samaria, and surveys famine, drought, blight, and war that God sent to turn Israel back, all without success. That repeated refrain, "yet have ye not returned unto me," builds toward the command in chapter 5 to seek the LORD while there is still time to live.

keyFigures.name: Prosperous women of Samaria
keyFigures.role: Group challenged by the prophet. Accused of oppressing the poor while pursuing consumption (Amos 4:1-3)

keyFigures.name: Israel (children of Israel)
keyFigures.role: Collective addressees. Continue religious observance without responding to warnings (Amos 4:4-12)

keyFigures.name: The LORD, God of hosts
keyFigures.role: Divine speaker and hymn subject. Both warns Israel and is described as creator and sovereign (Amos 4:6-13)

keyThemes.explanation: The wealthy women of Samaria are compared to well-fed cattle, demanding luxury from their husbands while the poor around them are crushed and oppressed (4:1-3).
Amos's sarcastic invitation to keep worshiping at Bethel and Gilgal exposes continued religious activity that only multiplies transgression instead of addressing it (4:4-5).

Five disasters, famine, drought, blight, plague, and military defeat, are each followed by the same refrain, that Israel still did not return to God, showing a pattern of hardened resistance rather than isolated misfortune (4:6-11).
The closing hymn names God as the one who forms mountains, creates wind, and turns day into night, grounding the command to prepare to meet him in his power over the whole created order (4:12-13).

Amos 5.summary: Amos sings a lament over the "virgin of Israel" as though she has already fallen (Amos 5:1–3). Nevertheless the call remains: seek the LORD and live, rather than relying on Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba (Amos 5:4–6). The indictment targets people who turn justice into bitterness, hate fair judgment in the gate, take bribes, and deprive the poor of justice (Amos 5:7, 10–13). The prophet contrasts seeking good with seeking evil and urges the people to establish justice (Amos 5:14–15). The "day of the LORD," expected by some as deliverance, will instead be darkness for those under judgment (Amos 5:18–20). God rejects festivals, songs, and sacrifices when righteousness is absent, and demands that justice roll on like waters (Amos 5:21–24). The chapter closes by recalling idolatry in the wilderness and warning of exile beyond Damascus (Amos 5:25–27). Its central argument is that true devotion cannot be separated from justice and ethical life.
Amos 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 ended with five warnings Israel failed to heed, each closing with the same refrain that the people had not returned to God (Amos 4:6–11). Chapter 5 responds with a funeral song for a nation Amos treats as already fallen, then pivots to an urgent appeal: seek the LORD and live, rather than trusting the shrines at Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba, and let justice replace the bribery corrupting the courts. That same contrast between hollow religion and real justice continues in chapter 6, which exposes the comfortable complacency of Israel's leaders in even sharper terms.

keyFigures.name: Israel (house of Israel)
keyFigures.role: People addressed in lament and exhortation. Urged to seek God and practice justice (Amos 5:1-27)

keyFigures.name: The LORD, God of hosts
keyFigures.role: Divine speaker. Calls for justice and rejects hollow worship (Amos 5:4-6,14-17,21-27)

keyFigures.name: Poor, just persons, and gate officials
keyFigures.role: Social groups in the accusation. Their mistreatment or responsibilities illustrate the legal corruption criticized (Amos 5:10-13)

keyThemes.explanation: Amos urges Israel to seek the LORD directly rather than at the shrines of Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba, since seeking the wrong thing leads to captivity instead of life (5:4-6).
Taking bribes and turning the poor away in the city gate, the public place where legal disputes were settled, corrupts the very institution meant to protect the vulnerable (5:10-15).

keyThemes.theme: False confidence in the day of the LORD
keyThemes.explanation: Some in Israel looked forward to the day of the LORD as a guaranteed victory; Amos warns it will instead be darkness for a people under judgment, like someone who escapes a lion only to meet a bear (5:18-20).

God declares that he hates festivals and sacrifices offered without justice, insisting that justice rolling down like waters describes what true devotion requires, not an optional addition to it (5:21-24).

explainedReferences.explanation: Amos about Israel's idolatry in the wilderness.

Amos 6.summary: Amos pronounces woe on those who are complacent in Zion and secure on Mount Samaria, challenging their claims to exceptional status (Amos 6:1–3). He describes influential people lounging on ivory-inlaid beds, eating choice meat, making music, drinking wine, and using fine oils without grieving over "the affliction of Joseph" (Amos 6:4–6). They will therefore be among the first taken away in exile (Amos 6:7). God declares hatred for their pride and palaces, and the chapter depicts severe death and devastation (Amos 6:8–11). Rhetorical questions about horses running on rocks and oxen plowing there expose the folly of transforming justice into poison and righteousness into bitterness (Amos 6:12). Leaders boast of military success at Lo-debar and Karnaim, but God announces an oppressing nation stretching from Lebo-hamath to the Arabah (Amos 6:13–14). Its focus is complacency, pride, and the failure of privileged people to confront communal suffering.
Amos 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 condemned worship that Israel kept up while abandoning justice in the courts (Amos 5:10–24). Chapter 6 turns to the leaders responsible for that imbalance, pronouncing woe on those who feel secure in Zion and Samaria, feast on the finest food and music, and feel no grief over the nation's coming ruin. Their complacency sets up the sharp break in chapter 7, where Amos moves from pronouncing judgment in general terms to a series of specific visions of exactly how it will arrive.

keyFigures.name: Secure leaders of Zion and Samaria
keyFigures.role: Complacent elites addressed. Trust in status, enjoyment, and prestige despite injustice (Amos 6:1-7)

keyFigures.name: House of Israel (house of Joseph)
keyFigures.role: Collective people affected. Their suffering and impending subjugation expose elite indifference (Amos 6:6-14)

keyFigures.name: The LORD God of hosts
keyFigures.role: Divine judge. Condemns arrogance and announces an oppressing nation (Amos 6:8,14)

keyThemes.explanation: Amos challenges people who feel secure in Zion and Samaria simply because of their city's reputation, exposing confidence based on status rather than on actual faithfulness (6:1-3).
Those who lounge on ivory beds, eat the finest food, and enjoy music and wine are condemned specifically for feeling no grief over the nation's own suffering around them (6:4-7).

Turning judgment into poison and righteousness into bitterness is as unnatural as horses running on bare rock, an image Amos uses to show how far Israel's courts have strayed from their purpose (6:12).

Leaders who boast of military victories are answered by God's announcement of an oppressing nation covering the whole land, showing that confidence built on past success cannot guarantee future safety (6:8, 6:13-14).

Amos 7.summary: The chapter moves to a sequence of visions and an encounter at Bethel. Amos first sees locusts consuming the land after the king's mowing, and pleads for Jacob, who is small; God relents from that announced disaster (Amos 7:1–3). In a second vision consuming fire threatens the land, and again Amos intercedes and the judgment is stayed (Amos 7:4–6). A third vision shows the LORD standing by a wall with a measuring tool, traditionally translated "plumbline"; this time judgment against Israel's sanctuaries and the house of Jeroboam is announced (Amos 7:7–9). Amaziah, priest of Bethel, reports Amos to Jeroboam and orders him to leave for Judah (Amos 7:10–13). Amos replies that he was a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs whom God commanded to prophesy, and foretells devastation for Amaziah's household and Israel's exile (Amos 7:14–17). The chapter combines intercession with mounting judgment and shows the struggle between royal religious authority and prophetic criticism.
Amos 7.whereWeAre: Chapter 6 pronounced woe on Israel's complacent leaders for ignoring the nation's coming ruin (Amos 6:1–14). Chapter 7 shows Amos receiving that judgment directly in a series of visions, twice persuading God to relent before a third vision announces judgment without reprieve, and shows the cost of delivering that message when Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, tries to send him home to Judah. Amos's reply that he was only a herdsman, not a professional prophet, carries into chapter 8, where another vision confirms that Israel's end has come.

keyFigures.name: Amos
keyFigures.role: Prophet and intercessor. Pleads for Jacob, sees visions, and defends his calling (Amos 7:1-17)

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Speaker in visions. Shows warnings and announces judgment (Amos 7:1-9,15-17)

keyFigures.name: Amaziah
keyFigures.role: Priest of Bethel. Accuses Amos of conspiracy and tries to expel him (Amos 7:10-17)

keyFigures.name: Jeroboam
keyFigures.role: King of Israel named in the confrontation. His royal house is named in the judgment and Amaziah reports Amos to him (Amos 7:9-11)

keyFigures.name: Jacob (Israel)
keyFigures.role: Collective people. Portrayed as vulnerable and subject to national judgment (Amos 7:2,5,8-9,17)

keyThemes.explanation: Amos twice pleads for Jacob, since he is small, and both times the LORD relents from judgment already announced, showing prayer actually changing what happens next (7:1-6).
The third vision of a plumbline against a crooked wall announces that the LORD will no longer pass by Israel's sin, ending the pattern of relenting seen in the first two visions (7:7-9).

Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, tries to send Amos back to Judah by appealing to royal authority, but Amos answers that he never sought the role and speaks only because the LORD commanded him to (7:10-15).
Because Amaziah tried to silence God's word, Amos announces specific, personal disaster for Amaziah's own household along with Israel's coming exile (7:16-17).

Amos 8.summary: Amos sees a basket of summer fruit, and a Hebrew wordplay links ripe fruit to the 'end' now approaching Israel (Amos 8:1–3). The prophet accuses merchants of wanting sacred days to finish so they can resume selling grain using dishonest measurements, inflated prices, and debt arrangements that exploit poor people; they even sell sweepings as wheat (Amos 8:4–6). The LORD declares that such behavior will not be forgotten (Amos 8:7). The prophetic picture then turns cosmic and communal: earth trembles, daylight darkens, songs become mourning, and festivities turn to grief (Amos 8:8–10). The gravest deprivation is described as a famine not of food but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11–12). Those seeking a word from God wander without success, while worship associated with Samaria, Dan, and Beersheba is condemned (Amos 8:13–14). The chapter teaches that persistent exploitation and resistance to the divine word culminate in loss rather than the security that prosperity appears to offer.
Amos 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 ended with Amos defending his calling against Amaziah's attempt to silence him and foretelling exile for Israel (Amos 7:14–17). Chapter 8 confirms that verdict with a vision of ripe summer fruit, a wordplay on Israel's own approaching end, then condemns merchants who cheat the poor with dishonest scales and can't wait for holy days to end so they can resume business. The chapter's most severe warning, a coming famine not of food but of hearing God's word, prepares for chapter 9's final vision, where no hiding place can escape the LORD at all.

keyFigures.name: Amos
keyFigures.role: Recipient of the fruit-basket vision. Reports the warning of Israel’s approaching end (Amos 8:1-3)

keyFigures.name: The LORD
keyFigures.role: Divine speaker. Declares knowledge of economic injustice and impending loss of revelation (Amos 8:1-12)

keyFigures.name: Merchants who oppress the needy
keyFigures.role: Accused economic actors. Manipulate weights, prices, and sale practices (Amos 8:4-6)

keyFigures.name: Poor and needy
keyFigures.role: Victims of exploitation. Those whose vulnerability exposes corruption (Amos 8:4-6)

keyFigures.name: Worshipers linked with Samaria, Dan and Beersheba
keyFigures.role: Idolatrous oath-makers addressed. Their religious confidence is declared unstable (Amos 8:13-14)

keyThemes.explanation: A basket of summer fruit becomes a wordplay on Israel's approaching end, since the Hebrew words for summer fruit and end sound alike, showing judgment as ripe and ready rather than distant (8:1-3).

Merchants eager for holy days to end so they can cheat customers with dishonest measures and even sell the sweepings as wheat show that Israel's injustice reaches into the details of ordinary commerce (8:4-6).
God promises to turn feasts into mourning and songs into lamentation, revealing that prosperity built on exploitation will end in grief rather than lasting security (8:7-10).

The gravest coming shortage is not bread or water but the words of the LORD; people will search for a message from God and not find one, having already rejected the warnings they were given (8:11-14).

Amos 9.summary: In a final vision Amos sees the LORD standing beside or on the altar and commanding a blow that shakes the structure; no hiding place, from the depths to the heights or beyond the sea, can escape the judgment (Amos 9:1–4). A hymn recalls divine command over land and sea (Amos 9:5–6). The LORD challenges Israel's presumption of uniqueness by recalling other peoples' migrations as well as Israel's exodus (Amos 9:7). Yet judgment will not mean complete annihilation: the sinful kingdom will be shaken, and sinners who deny approaching disaster will fall (Amos 9:8–10). The tone then changes to restoration: God promises to raise up "the tabernacle of David that is fallen," repair its ruins, and renew the fortunes of the people (Amos 9:11–15). The final images are of plentiful harvest, rebuilt cities, vineyards, gardens, and secure planting in their land. The chapter holds warning and hope together; interpretation of the restored Davidic rule and the status of surrounding nations varies among Jewish and Christian readers.
Amos 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 warned of a coming famine of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11–12). Chapter 9 delivers the book's final vision: no hiding place, from the depths of the sea to the heights of heaven, can shelter those under judgment, yet the LORD promises Israel will not be destroyed completely. The book closes with hope instead of ruin, promising to raise up David's fallen house and resettle the people in their own land, before Obadiah, the next book, turns to a single judgment oracle against Edom alone.

keyFigures.name: The LORD God of hosts
keyFigures.role: Speaker and visionary figure. Pronounces judgment and promises future restoration (Amos 9:1-15)

keyFigures.name: Israel (house of Jacob)
keyFigures.role: Collective addressees. Face sifting and judgment yet receive a restoration promise (Amos 9:7-15)

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Earlier royal ancestor named in an image. His fallen tabernacle stands for a future restoration associated with Davidic rule (Amos 9:11)

keyFigures.name: Edom and nations called by God’s name
keyFigures.role: Peoples named in a restoration oracle. Their relation to the restored rule depends in part on textual and interpretive questions (Amos 9:12)

keyThemes.explanation: Whether sinners dig into the earth, climb to heaven, or hide at the bottom of the sea, Amos insists none of these places can shelter them from the LORD (9:1-4).

God's rule over creation and his bringing other peoples, the Philistines from Caphtor and the Syrians from Kir, out of their own lands just as he brought Israel from Egypt, challenges any assumption that Israel's relationship with God guarantees special treatment (9:5-8).
Even as the sinful kingdom is shaken, God promises not to utterly destroy the house of Jacob, holding judgment and survival together rather than letting judgment mean total annihilation (9:8-10).
The book ends by promising to raise up David's fallen house and restore abundant harvests and secure, permanent settlement, answering eight chapters of judgment with genuine hope (9:11-15).

explainedReferences.explanation: Amos about restoring David's fallen dwelling.
